newsitem.title: USA: Enron competitive under U.K. J-Block pact.
newsitem.headline: Enron competitive under U.K. J-Block pact.

text.p: Enron Corp executives on Monday said a "significant amount" of natural gas to be supplied to the company under its revised J-Block contract in the North Sea has already been marketed.

"A significant amount of the gas has already been marketed longer term," Enron Chairman Ken Lay said of the company's settlement of a long-running contract dispute with J-Block producers in the United Kingdom.
"The important thing is we believe what we agreed to here gets the price of this gas down to a level where we can be competitive in the U.K. market going forward," Lay said.

Enron agreed to pay $440 million to J-Block producers to settle litigation and amend a take-or-pay contract to a firm, long-term supply contract with a reduced price on gas to be lifted from the U.K. North Sea sector.
"For all intents and purposes, this is a 15-year contract," Enron President Jeffrey Skilling said. Other terms of the amended contract were not disclosed.

The initial take-or-pay contract became uneconomical for the Houston-based company when two of its U.K. power projects to be fueled with the gas were delayed and North Sea natural gas prices subsequently fell, Lay said.

Lay indicated Enron paid less under the settlement than it would have had it taken the gas under terms of the initial contract, but he declined to comment further when asked if the company was better off financially with the settlement.
"We are, and I think that's enough be said on that," he said.

Enron said it will post a $450 million after-tax or $1.80 a share second quarter charge to cover costs of the settlement, including the cash payment to J-Block producers Phillips Petroleum Co's Phillips U.K., BG Exploration and Production Ltd and Agip (U.K.) Ltd.

Lay said Phillips' decision to begin reinjecting associated gas back into the field so it could begin crude oil production "really just introduced one more level of litigation which made the whole process more complicated."
Lay said he expected the settlement to lift a cloud of uncertainty that has hung over Enron's stock this year, depressing its share price on the New York Stock Exchange.

"We think in fact (the settlement) ought to be a positive, because on an uncertainty like this the market tends to fear the worst," he said. "We're delighted to get this uncertainty removed from the company and the stock price of the company."
